Secondly, these actors have to make publicly available a summary of the content used for the training of their models in order to “facilitate parties with legitimate interests, including copyright holders, to exercise and enforce their rights under Union law” (Art. 53(1)(d) AI Act).Footnote 2 Shortly before these provisions became applicable on 2 August 2025, the European Commission published a whole package of documents that concretise these rather general statutory obligations: draft Guidelines on the scope of application of the GPAIM Chapter of the AI Act,Footnote 3 a Template for the public summary of training content,Footnote 4 and a GPAI Code of Practice (CoP) with a Transparency, a Copyright and a Safety and Security Chapter.Footnote 5 The Copyright Chapter of the GPAI CoP is the topic of this article. The GPAI CoP was drawn up in accordance with Art. 56 AI Act as a unique form of co-regulation.Footnote 6 It was neither drafted in a self-regulatory manner by GPAIM providers nor by the Commission, but by “independent experts” including the authors of this article, who had been appointed by the European Commission.Footnote 7 The iterative drafting process started in July 2024 with a stakeholder consultation and an invitation to participate in the drawing-up of the Code,Footnote 8 and continued over the following months with three published drafts of the CodeFootnote 9 and repeated feedback by providers, rightsholders and other civil society stakeholders, Member States, Members of the European Parliament and, last but not least, the AI Office and the Commission’s Copyright Unit.Footnote 10 The final version of the Code was published on 10 July 2025.Footnote 11 Twenty-six GPAIM providers have since then become Signatories to the Code, including major European and US model providers such as Aleph Alpha, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, Mistral and OpenAI.Footnote 12 On 1 August 2025, the European Commission and the AI Board as the AI Act institution representing the Member States published their assessments that the Code adequately covers the obligations pursuant to Arts. 53 and 55 AI Act.Footnote 13 Following this positive assessment, the Signatories to the Copyright Chapter can now “demonstrate compliance” with the copyright policy obligation under Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act by adhering to the code, whereas non-Signatories will have to demonstrate alternative adequate means of compliance for assessment by the Commission.Footnote 14 2 Commentary of the Copyright Chapter of the GPAI CoP In the following, we provide a commentary-style explanation of the Copyright Chapter of the GPAI CoP, whose text is reproduced in italics. 2.1 General Objectives of the Code Objectives The overarching objective of this Code of Practice (“Code”) is to improve the functioning of the internal market, to promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence (“AI”), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law, and environmental protection, against harmful effects of AI in the Union, and to support innovation pursuant to Article 1(1) AI Act. To achieve this overarching objective, the specific objectives of this Code are: A. To serve as a guiding document for demonstrating compliance with the obligations provided for in Articles 53 and 55 AI Act, while recognising that adherence to the Code does not constitute conclusive evidence of compliance with these obligations under the AI Act. B. To ensure providers of general-purpose AI models comply with their obligations under the AI Act and to enable the AI Office to assess compliance of providers of general-purpose AI models who choose to rely on the Code to demonstrate compliance with their obligations under the AI Act. The Copyright Chapter of the GPAI CoP is structured in three parts: Objectives, Recitals and one Commitment with five accessory Measures.Footnote 15 The Objectives articulate the purpose of the Code as such. They form part of all three Chapters of the Code in an identical manner. This repetitive structure is the consequence of a de facto division of the Code into three separate parts. While the Code was drawn up in one process, presented as a whole in all prior drafts and assessed and still referred to by the Commission and the AI Board as one single text,Footnote 16 the final version was published in three separate documents: the Transparency Chapter, the Copyright Chapter, and the Safety and Security Chapter.Footnote 17 The three Chapters indeed differ in their respective scope of application and purpose. The Transparency Chapter addresses competition and enforcement-related concerns and does not apply to free and open-source models (FOSMs).Footnote 18 Article 53(1)(c) AI Act and the Copyright Chapter respond to the “challenges” that GPAIMs, including FOSMs, present to artists, authors, and other creators and the way their creative content is created, distributed, used and consumed.Footnote 19 The Safety and Security Chapter only applies to GPAIMs that the Commission has formally confirmed to display “high impact capabilities” that can trigger “systemic risks”.Footnote 20 The three Chapters of the Code were also “separately authored” by the responsible chairs and vice-chairs.Footnote 21 Last but not least, strategic considerations might have led the Commission to practically split up the Code because this solution increases the adoption rate of the Code by granting more flexibility to GPAIM providers. xAI is the example on point. It only signed up to the Safety and Security Chapter and therefore will have to demonstrate compliance with the AI Act’s obligations concerning transparency and copyright via alternative adequate means.Footnote 22 It is unclear whether the Commission would also accept a signature that is limited to the Transparency or Copyright Chapter. On the one hand, these two Chapters apply to all GPAIMs and not only to GPAIMs with systemic risk, but on the other hand, their scope of application differs with regard to FOSM.Footnote 23 The Code is meant to contribute to the “proper application” of the AI Act.Footnote 24 Consequently, the first sentence of the Objectives incorporates the wording of Art. 1(1) AI Act nearly verbatim to articulate the “overarching” aim of the Code. The second sentence formulates two “specific” objectives of the Code as a co-regulatory tool supplementing the AI Act. Point A takes the perspective of the addressees of the Code, i.e. providers of GPAIMs. For them, the three Chapters serve as “guiding documents” and “significant benchmarks” for their compliance with Arts. 53 and 55 AI Act.Footnote 25 However, adherence to the Code is merely a means to “demonstrate compliance” (cf. Art. 53(4) AI Act), without constituting “conclusive” evidence of compliance. In other words, even the full compliance of a GPAIM provider with the Copyright Chapter does not automatically mean full compliance with Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act. For example, a provider who excludes piracy websites from its crawling activities in line with Measure 1.2(1)(b) but obtains large pirated datasets such as so-called “shadow libraries” by other means from third parties in order to train its models can hardly claim to have put in place a sufficient copyright policy. Copyright-infringing activities that are equivalent to the ones ruled out by the Code but not covered by the Code should generally be considered an indicator of an insufficient copyright policy and thus a violation of Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act. Point B adds a public policy and enforcement perspective on the Code, which represents “a central tool” to ensure “proper compliance” of model providers with their AI Act obligations by specifying the concrete measures a provider has to take and by therefore establishing clear thresholds for the assessment of their actions by the AI Office.Footnote 26 In its Guidelines on the scope of GPAIM provider obligations, the Commission explains how this win-win-situation will play out. Whereas Code Signatories will benefit from increased trust and can presume that the Commission will focus its enforcement on monitoring adherence to the Code,Footnote 27 non-Signatories must expect to be subject to more information requests upon which they will have to explain and demonstrate how they comply via other adequate means.Footnote 28 In this way, the Code can reduce the compliance and enforcement costs of providers and the AI Office alike. 2.2 Recitals to the Copyright Chapter (a) 1This Chapter aims to contribute to the proper application of the obligation laid down in Article 53(1), point (c), of the AI Act pursuant to which providers that place general-purpose AI models on the Union market must put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights, and in particular to identify and comply with, including through state-of-the-art technologies, a reservation of rights expressed by rightsholders pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790. 2While Signatories will implement the Measures set out in this Chapter in order to demonstrate compliance with Article 53(1), point (c), of the AI Act, adherence to the Code does not constitute compliance with Union law on copyright and related rights. (b) This Chapter in no way affects the application and enforcement of Union law on copyright and related right which is for the courts of Member States and ultimately the Court of Justice of the European Union to interpret. (c) The Signatories hereby acknowledge that Union law on copyright and related rights: (i) is provided for in directives addressed to Member States and that for present purposes Directive 2001/29/EC, Directive (EU) 2019/790 and Directive 2004/48/EC are the most relevant; (ii) provides for exclusive rights that are preventive in nature and thus is based on prior consent save where an exception or limitation applies; (iii) provides for an exception or limitation for text and data mining in Article 4(1) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 which shall apply on conditions of lawful access and that the use of works and other subject matter referred to in that paragraph has not been expressly reserved by their rightsholders in an appropriate manner pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790. (d) The commitments in this Chapter that require proportionate measures should be commensurate and proportionate to the size of providers, taking due account of the interests of SMEs, including startups. (e) This Chapter does not affect agreements between the Signatories and rightsholders authorising the use of works and other protected subject matter. (f) The commitments in this Chapter to demonstrate compliance with the obligation under Article 53(1), point (c), of the AI Act are complementary to the obligation of providers under Article 53(1), point (d), of the AI Act to draw up and make publicly available sufficiently detailed summaries about the content used by the Signatories for the training of their general-purpose AI models, according to a template to be provided by the AI Office. In contrast to the overarching, generic “Objectives” of the Code, the following six Recitals are specific to the Copyright Chapter. None of these Recitals sets out an operational commitment. Instead, they explain how the Copyright Chapter is to be applied and interpreted. The first sentence of point (a) ties the general purpose of the Code, namely to “contribute to the proper application” of Chapter V of the AI Act (Art. 56(1) AI Act), to a particular obligation, namely the one laid down in Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act, which is then quoted in full. Thus, the purpose of the Copyright Chapter is to concretise what it means to “put in place a policy to comply” with Union law on copyright and related rights (in the following: Union copyright law). Several further Recitals address the relationship between the Code and Union copyright law. The latter’s core features are summarised in point (c). Point (i) lists the three most relevant Directives regarding AI, namely the Information Society,Footnote 29 the Digital Single MarketFootnote 30 and the Enforcement Directive.Footnote 31 Point (ii) recalls that these directives set out exclusive rights that are preventive in nature and are thus based on prior consent save where an exception or limitation applies (point (ii).) Finally, point (iii) highlights the text and data mining (TDM) provision of Art. 4 of the Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive (CDSMD) with its conditions of lawful access and appropriate rights reservations, which is also referenced in Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act (point (iii)). Signatories “acknowledge” that these restatements of EU law are correct. While this acknowledgment does not create a new basis for infringement claims of rightsholders, it affirms that Signatories have to observe the relevant rules of the directives, which normally only bind Member States.Footnote 32 Point (c)(ii) furthermore clarifies what it means to “comply with” Union copyright law, namely, in essence, to either operate within the boundaries of an exception or limitation (in particular Art. 4 CDSMD) or to abstain from a use for which no prior authorisation has been obtained.Footnote 33 Thus, the objective of a “policy to comply” with Union copyright law is to prevent copyright infringements.Footnote 34 In contrast, Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act does not create an obligation to enter into license contracts because Union copyright law does not impose such an obligation in the context of GPAIMs.Footnote 35 Point (a) second sentence and point (b) accentuate the need to distinguish between the Code and Union copyright law.Footnote 36 According to point (a), adherence to the Code does not constitute compliance with Union copyright law. Thus, even if a model provider has implemented a copyright policy that is fully compliant with the Code and the AI Act, potentially remaining copyright infringements still trigger all applicable copyright remedies.Footnote 37 Point (b) states the logical consequence that the Copyright Chapter “in no way affects the application and enforcement” of Union copyright law, “which is for the courts of Member States and ultimately the Court of Justice of the European Union to interpret”.Footnote 38 Indeed, a co-regulatory Code of Practice cannot modify pre-existing EU directives in any way. Vice versa, EU copyright law merely functions a point of reference of the AI Act and the Code. It defines the rules that the copyright policy of GPAIM providers has to ensure compliance with – without itself becoming part of AI law.Footnote 39 Article 53(1)(c) AI Act did not create a “fusion”, “amalgamation” or “mix” of AI law and copyright law.Footnote 40 GPAIM providers have to comply with both bodies of law, and rightsholders can benefit from the supervision of the GPAIM market by the AI Office, in addition to the conventional enforcement of their private rights in individual cases.Footnote 41 Point (e) of the Recitals articulates another consequence of the distinction between AI law and copyright law by confirming that the Code does not affect agreements between the Signatories and rightsholders authorising the use of works and other protected subject matter. Under international and Union copyright law, transactions regarding copyright-protected content form the “normal” mode of exploitation.Footnote 42 The possibility of rightsholders to reserve and then licence commercial TDM uses in accordance with Art. 4 CDSMD mirrors this market-based approach.Footnote 43 GPAIM providers also benefit from agreements with rightsholders by gaining legal certainty and potentially exclusive access to high-quality training data. Accordingly, obtaining an authorisation from the relevant rightsholders is the most straightforward way of complying with copyright law and thereby also with the obligation under Art. 53(1)(c) of the AI Act. In such a situation, the obligations of a GPAIM provider are primarily defined by the respective commercial agreement. GPAIM provider activity that is covered by a valid authorisation need not align with the Measures set out in the Code because and insofar as copyright compliance is already guaranteed through the agreement. Point (d) concerns the proportionality of copyright compliance measures. The principle of proportionality features prominently in the AI Act and is also not completely alien to Union copyright law.Footnote 44 GPAIM providers are only required to put in place measures to comply with Union copyright law that are, overall, proportionate. In this context, recital 109 second sentence AI Act states that compliance with the obligations under Art. 53(1) AI Act “should take due account of the size of the provider and allow simplified ways of compliance for SMEs, including start-ups, that should not represent an excessive cost and not discourage the use of such models”. Point (d) specifies in which constellations the size of a GPAIM provider is relevant for assessing adherence to the Code. It provides that “commitments that require proportionate measures should be commensurate and proportionate to the size of providers, taking due account of the interests of SMEs, including startups”. The only commitment on point is Measure 1.4(1)(a) regarding “appropriate and proportionate technical safeguards to prevent … models from generating outputs that reproduce training content … in an infringing manner”. It follows that the size of a Signatory is relevant only for assessing the proportionality of its technical output safeguards while all other Measures have to be adhered to irrespective of the size of a Signatory. The special role of Measure 1.4(1)(a) is justified by the potential costs associated with the generic commitment to actively implement and keep up-to-date technical solutions such as output filters. While these costs depend on aspects such as the availability of technologies that lie at least partly beyond the control of a Signatory, the other Measures appear proportionate for Signatories of all sizes because they merely rule out certain infringing activities (Measure 1.2), require limited organisational steps (Measures 1.1(1), 1.4.(1)(b), 1.5), the adoption of low-cost technical solutions (Measure 1.3(1)(a) [robots.txt] and (4) [web feed]), or are subject to pending standardisation procedures, which have to result in technically feasible/implementable solutions (Measure 1.3(1)(a) [future robots.txt version] and (b) [future opt-out protocols]). Point (f) concerns the relationship between the Copyright Chapter and the obligation of GPAIM providers to draw up and make publicly available a summary of their training content according to the Template provided by the AI Office pursuant to Art. 53(1)(d) AI Act.Footnote 45 These two sets of rules overlap teleologically but were prepared in separate processes. While the Copyright Chapter is the result of an iterative, multistakeholder drafting process, the Template was provided “in house” by the AI Office.Footnote 46 The legal effects of the Copyright Chapter and the Template also differ. The Copyright Chapter is a voluntary tool for GPAIM providers who want to demonstrate their compliance with Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act by adhering to the Code. The Template, in contrast, has to be filled in and made publicly available at the latest when a GPAIM is placed on the Union market by all GPAIM providers, regardless of whether they are Signatories to the Code of Practice or not.Footnote 47 Irrespective of these differences, the Code and the Template should be applied and interpreted in a complementary manner that supports the “proper application” of both underlying AI Act obligations. For example, Measure 1.3(4) complements the transparency about TDM opt-out compliance according to Sec. 3.1 of the Template in that it requires the publication of relevant information already “at the time of crawling” (and not only ex post at the time of market placement as per the Template) and with “a means for affected rightsholders to be automatically notified when such information is updated (such as by syndicating a web feed)”.Footnote 48 Conversely, the Template requires transparency also regarding training data sources not covered by the Copyright Chapter, in particular publicly available and private datasets obtained from third parties.Footnote 49 This obligatory transparency indirectly fosters compliance with the copyright policy obligation pursuant to Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act. For example, if a training content summary lists a dataset that a provider who acts in accordance with high industry standards of professional diligenceFootnote 50 would have identified as a structurally infringing, pirated dataset, the respective provider can hardly be said to have put in place a sufficient copyright policy as required by Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act.Footnote 51 2.3 Commitment 1 Copyright Policy (1) 1In order to demonstrate compliance with their obligation pursuant to Article 53(1), point (c) of the AI Act to put in place a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights, and in particular to identify and comply with, including through state-of-the-art technologies, a reservation of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790, Signatories commit to drawing up, keeping up-to-date and implementing such a copyright policy. 2The Measures below do not affect compliance with Union law on copyright and related rights. 3They set out commitments by which the Signatories can demonstrate compliance with the obligation to put in place a copyright policy for their general-purpose AI models they place on the Union market. (2) In addition, the Signatories remain responsible for verifying that the Measures included in their copyright policy as outlined below comply with Member States’ implementation of Union law on copyright and related rights, in particular but not only Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790, before carrying out any copyright-relevant act in the territory of the relevant Member State as failure to do so may give rise to liability under Union law on copyright and related rights. The operative part of the Copyright Chapter consists of one Commitment (C1) and five accessory Measures.Footnote 52 Like the other Chapters, the Copyright Chapter does not provide for key performance indicators (KPIs). Such KPIs were contained in the second draft of the Code but were dropped thereafter because the AI Act does not unconditionally require them, and the measures were considered sufficiently precise in and of themselves to not warrant additional indicators of performance.Footnote 53 C1(1) first sentence contains the single copyright-related commitment and articulates its legal effect: Signatories commit to drawing up, keeping up-to-date and implementing a copyright policy in line with Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act in order to “demonstrate compliance” with this statutory obligation.Footnote 54 The second and third sentences of C1(1) repeat caveats to this somewhat circular statement, which are already set out in the overall Objectives and the Recitals of the Copyright Chapter. The following five Copyright Measures (the “Measures below”) neither affect conventional copyright complianceFootnote 55 nor do they “constitute conclusive evidence of compliance” with Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act.Footnote 56 Instead, the Copyright Measures represent the cumulative minimum a Signatory has to fulfil in order to be able to demonstrate compliance with its copyright policy obligation. The Code does not offer a menu of optional measures. Either a Signatory commits to and actually adheres to the full set of Measures or it does not in fact rely on the Code as a whole and therefore cannot demonstrate compliance with Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act. For example, a Signatory who is not transparent in real time about its crawlers or who does not enable the lodging of complaints does not deserve the trust that a Code signature generally justifies.Footnote 57 C1(1) third sentence in fine provides that the Copyright Chapter applies to all GPAIMs that a provider places on the Union market.Footnote 58 The notions of a provider and of a GPAIM are defined in Art. 3 AI Act and further specified in Commission Guidelines on the scope of application of Chapter V of the AI Act.Footnote 59 These Guidelines confirm that the models that triggered the copyright-related rules of the AI Act, namely “large generative AI models, capable of generating text, images, and other content” (recital 105 AI Act), will indeed typically be covered by the Copyright Chapter. Models whose training compute is greater than 1023 FLOP and that can generate language in the form of text (including code), audio (including speech), text-to-image or text-to-video will generally be considered a GPAIM for which a copyright policy must be put in place. In contrast, models trained specifically for distinct tasks such as transcribing speech, generating speech from text, increasing the resolution of images, playing games or modelling weather patterns or physical systems will likely not be qualified as GPAIMs, but also do not present particular copyright challenges.Footnote 60 More problematic from a copyright perspective is the example of a model that is capable of generating “music based on text prompts including lyrics”, which the Commission also considers a “simple” model to which Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act would not apply.Footnote 61 Copyright issues regarding such a model would consequently be governed by conventional copyright law only. Signatories commit to put in place a copyright policy for every GPAIM “they place on the Union market”.Footnote 62 The latter phrase is taken from Art. 2(a) AI Act, which proclaims that the AI Act including Art. 53(1)(c) applies to “providers … placing on the market general-purpose AI models in the Union, irrespective of whether those providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country”.Footnote 63 A GPAIM is “placed on the market” if it is “made available” for the first time “on the Union market”, i.e. supplied “for distribution or use on the Union market in the course of a commercial activity, whether in return for payment or free of charge”.Footnote 64 By referring to the placement of a GPAIM on the Union market as the point of attachment that triggers its applicability, the Copyright Chapter confirms that the Code follows an AI law and not a copyright law logic regarding its territorial scope of application.Footnote 65 These logics differ fundamentally. Whereas Union copyright law attaches to the use of a protected content so that reproductions during the training stage are only subject to EU copyright law if they occur on Union territory,Footnote 66 the AI Act addresses potential harms of AI systems and models and therefore establishes market entry conditions that have to be observed irrespective of where the AI system or model was developed.Footnote 67 The question whether and to what extent this product safety, effects-based approach creates a conflict with copyright law’s territoriality principle is hotly debated.Footnote 68 As we have explained above, Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act refers to Union copyright law as the subject matter of this obligation but neither belongs to copyright law nor creates a novel fusion of AI/copyright law. The obligation it establishes is a general, preventive one that is abstract from concrete copyright infringements and the national laws governing them under the rule of lex loci protectionis.Footnote 69 Recital 106 sentence 2 explicitly states that providers should comply with Art. 53(1)(c) “regardless of the jurisdiction in which the copyright-relevant acts underpinning the training of those general-purpose AI models take place”. This effect is not justified with a copyright argumentFootnote 70 but with the necessity “to ensure a level playing field among providers of general-purpose AI models where no provider should be able to gain a competitive advantage in the Union market by applying lower copyright standards than those provided in the Union” – i.e. with an Internal Market argument.Footnote 71 Training in third countries remains subject to the copyright laws of those third countries.Footnote 72 The territoriality principle of international copyright law thus remains unaffected. As long as the GPAIM developed on the basis of third-country training is not placed on the Union market, Chapter V of the AI Act is also inapplicable. However, as soon as such a model enters the EU market, the copyright policy obligation and the Copyright Commitment kick in and must be applied throughout the entire lifecycle of the model.Footnote 73 The market placement does not only trigger commitments ex nunc, for example regarding technical safeguards to prevent output infringements (Measure 1.4(1)(a)) or a mechanism to allow the submission of complaints (Measure 1.5(2)), but also Measures 1.2 and 1.3 that regulate the use of web-crawlers for training purposes, an activity that logically predates the market entry. The ensuing retroactive effect of the market entry is not unique to the copyright policy obligation but concerns all obligations under Chapter V.Footnote 74 It mirrors a product safety logic, which targets the development of AI systems and models, irrespective of where this “production” occurred.Footnote 75 Ultimately, EU AI law forces providers to take a decision about a possible release of a future GPAIM in the EU and accordingly about its compliance with the AI Act already before a new model is developed, i.e. prior to the start of a pre-training run.Footnote 76 As regards GPAIMs that had been placed on the EU market before 2 August 2025, providers have to take the “necessary steps” in order to comply with Chapter V of the AI Act by 2 August 2027.Footnote 77 While the Commission does not expect a “retraining or unlearning of models, where it is not possible to do this for actions performed in the past”, such limitations of ex post compliance “must be clearly disclosed and justified in the copyright policy and in the summary of the content used for training”.Footnote 78 C1(2) proclaims that “in addition” to their AI law obligation, Signatories “remain responsible for verifying” that their copyright policy measures comply with Member States’ implementations of EU copyright directives before they carry out copyright-relevant acts in the territory of a Member State. Although this provision differs from all other references to copyright law in the CodeFootnote 79 in that it positively states that Signatories have a “responsibility” to comply with national copyright laws, it is nonetheless just another non-operational reminder of the AI law/copyright law distinction already explained above.Footnote 80 C1(2) does not imply a commitment to draw up and implement 27 copyright policy versions that correspond to all Member States’ copyright laws. Instead, it just highlights that failure to fully comply with Member States’ laws may give rise to copyright liability if infringements occur “in the territory of the relevant Member State”. Conversely, such infringements do not automatically translate into a non-compliance with the Code and Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act, which have to be assessed separately. EU AI law only requires one single copyright policy, which has to correspond to the (minimum) level of protection that EU copyright directives establish.Footnote 81 If Member States enjoy discretion in how to implement a directive,Footnote 82 Signatories are equally free to base their copyright policy on any such interpretation. They cannot be forced, via Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act in connection with C1(2), to align their copyright policy with one particular reading of a directive, even if failure to do so results in infringements in certain (or even all) Member States. 2.4 Measure 1.1 Draw Up, Keep Up-to-Date and Implement a Copyright Policy (1) 1Signatories will draw up, keep up-to-date and implement a policy to comply with Union law on copyright and related rights for all general-purpose AI models they place on the Union market. 2Signatories commit to describe that policy in a single document incorporating the Measures set out in this Chapter. 3Signatories will assign responsibilities within their organisation for the implementation and overseeing of this policy. (2) Signatories are encouraged to make publicly available and keep up-to-date a summary of their copyright policy. Measure 1.1 formulates, in generic terms, what a Signatory has to do in order to “put in place” a copyright policy.Footnote 83 The following four measures then detail the concrete steps that such a policy has to incorporate so that a Signatory can demonstrate compliance with Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act.Footnote 84 The first sentence of Measure 1.1(1) repeats the fundamental commitment already proclaimed in C1(1), namely that Signatories will draw up, keep up-to-date and implement a copyright policy. The act of drawing up an internal policy refers to the drafting of the policy and its adoption by the internally responsible body or officer. The copyright policy must be described in a single document that covers all Measures set out in the Copyright Chapter.Footnote 85 The purpose of this formal requirement is to support internal compliance through a comprehensive collection of all necessary steps. Signatories should have fulfilled this basic commitment as of 2 August 2025, when Chapter V of the AI Act entered into force, irrespective of the fact that the Commission will only start enforcing Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act from 2 August 2026 onwards with regard to GPAIMs that are not fully compliant “on that date”.Footnote 86 The commitment to keep the adopted policy up-to-dateFootnote 87 requires that Signatories date and version their policy and that they actively follow relevant technological and legal developments and amend their policy without undue delay if necessary. A need for updates arises, for example, if a new version of the robots.txt protocol or other appropriate machine-readable opt-out protocols are adopted in accordance with Measure 1.3(1)(a) or (b) or if the CJEU interprets the copyright acquis in a way that differs from the assumptions underlying the Code and a respective internal policy. Finally, Signatories must implement, i.e. give effect to their copyright policy.Footnote 88 This includes, according to the final sentence of M1.1(1), that Signatories assign responsibilities within their organisation for the implementation and overseeing of their copyright policy. The copyright policy document should identify the respective internal unit(s) and their reporting obligations in the case of an observed violation of the policy.Footnote 89 The internal copyright unit has to ensure that the policy is observed throughout the entire lifecycle of every GPAIM that has or might be released in the EU.Footnote 90 Indeed, diligent enforcement of the copyright policy is particularly important at the planning stage of a new GPAIM, when decisions about the training sources and possible output features of the model are made. The copyright unit also appears best placed to handle complaints lodged in accordance with Measure 1.5(2), which may indicate existing compliance deficits. Paragraph 2 encourages Signatories to voluntarily make a summary of their copyright policy publicly available and keep it up-to-date.Footnote 91 Ideally, this summary would be posted on the same website that informs about the opt-out measures respected by a Signatory, its point of contact and the possibility to submit Code-related complaints.Footnote 92 However, Signatories who do not publish a summary of their copyright policy can nonetheless claim to adhere to the Code in order to demonstrate compliance with Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act. Firstly, neither the AI Act nor Union copyright law require such transparency.Footnote 93 Point (c) of Art. 53(1) AI Act obliges providers to “put in place” a copyright policy, and point (d) requires public transparency only regarding the “content used for training” a GPAIM, not as regards the policy pursuant to point (c).Footnote 94 Secondly, the publication of a summary of the copyright policy does not, in itself, prevent infringements. This, however, is what a copyright policy in line with Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act must aim at.Footnote 95 2.5 Measure 1.2. Reproduce and Extract Only Lawfully Accessible Copyright-Protected Content When Crawling the World Wide Web (1) 1In order to help ensure that Signatories only reproduce and extract lawfully accessible works and other protected subject matter if they use web-crawlers or have such web-crawlers used on their behalf to scrape or otherwise compile data for the purpose of text and data mining as defined in Article 2(2) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 and the training of their general-purpose AI models, Signatories commit: (a) not to circumvent effective technological measures as defined in Article 6(3) of Directive 2001/29/EC that are designed to prevent or restrict unauthorised acts in respect of works and other protected subject matter, in particular by respecting any technological denial or restriction of access imposed by subscription models or paywalls, and (b) to exclude from their web-crawling websites that make available to the public content and which are, at the time of web-crawling, recognised as persistently and repeatedly infringing copyright and related rights on a commercial scale by courts or public authorities in the European Union and the European Economic Area. 2For the purpose of compliance with this measure, a dynamic list of hyperlinks to lists of these websites issued by the relevant bodies in the European Union and the European Economic Area will be made publicly available on an EU website. The Measure consists of two parts: the introductory paragraph outlines the objective and the scope of application, while points (a) and (b) set out the concrete measures to be taken.Footnote 96 The purpose of this Measure is to “help ensure” that Signatories comply with Art. 4(1) of the CDSMD, which allows for “reproductions and extractions of lawfully accessible” content for text and data mining. The wording “help ensure” indicates that even full compliance with the Measure might not be enough to fully prevent the use of protected content that is not lawfully accessible and thus not permitted under Art. 4 CDSMD. Measure 2.2 also does not settle the hotly debated question of whether reproductions (Art. 2 of Directive (EC) 2001/29) and extractions (Art. 7 of Directive (EC) 1996/9) made during GPAI web-crawling activities qualify as permissible text and data mining under Art. 4 of Directive (EU) 2019/790.Footnote 97 The Code of Practice cannot and does not answer this question, as it is ultimately for the CJEU to decide.Footnote 98 It therefore phrases the measure in a conditional manner: the measure only applies “if” Signatories crawl and compile data for the purpose of text and data mining as defined in Art. 2(2) of Directive (EU) 2019/790. Although the inclusion of measures 1.2 and 1.3 in the Code indicates that the Code is based on the assumption that Art. 4 CDSMD, which is expressly referenced in Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act, is indeed of relevance in the context of GPAIM training, the measures will run idle “if” the CJEU found that GPAIM training does not qualify as potentially permissible TDM. If Art. 4 applies, it also applies by definition to providers who are commercial actors even if they train on a database collected on the basis of Art. 3 CDSMD (TDM for scientific research purposes), such as the LAION database,Footnote 99 because commercial actors do not benefit from Art. 3 and cannot do so indirectly “by delegating [their] TDM activities to a public research institution”.Footnote 100 Allowing for such an indirect benefit would amount to “data washing”Footnote 101 or “data laundering”.Footnote 102 It is therefore important that “clear distinctions […] be made between the TDM undertaken by dataset providers that may benefit from Article 3 or 4”Footnote 103 in order to facilitate compliance. There is also considerable legal uncertainty as to what “lawfully accessible” in the sense of Art. 4(1) CDSMD means.Footnote 104 To this end, it is helpful to consider international standards,Footnote 105 especially the US fair use exception.Footnote 106 “Lawful access” in the US has been interpreted to exclude the use of training datasets that contain pirated works or works accessed by circumventing paywalls.Footnote 107 As for the scope of application, Measure 1.2 covers the crawling of the World Wide Web, carried out by or on behalf of a Signatory, for the purpose of collecting data to train a GPAIM, which is the typical mode of collecting vast amounts of data from the internet.Footnote 108 It covers crawling as a means to scrape, or compile data for the purpose of text and data mining as defined in Art. 2(2) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 and the training of GPAIMs. Although crawling and scraping are technically similar processes, they differ significantly in their intended purposes and legal consequences (see the discussion in Section 2.2.2).Footnote 109 The purpose of the data collection should align with TDM as defined in Art. 2(2), which refers to “any automated analytical technique aimed at analysing text and data in digital form in order to generate information which includes but is not limited to patterns, trends and correlations”. Measure 1.2 does not cover other modes of data acquisition, such as the acquisition of pre-existing “datasets”.Footnote 110 Points (a) and (b) describe the concrete measures to help ensure compliance with the condition of lawful access. Point (a) requires Signatories to not circumvent effective technological protection measures (TPM) as defined in Art. 6(3) of Directive 2001/29/EC. Art. 6(1) of the InfoSoc Directive states that: “Member States shall provide adequate legal protection against the circumvention of any effective technological measures, which the person concerned carries out in the knowledge, or with reasonable grounds to know, that he or she is pursuing that objective.” Article 6(3) adds that “the expression ‘technological measures’ means any technology, device or component that, in the normal course of its operation, is designed to prevent or restrict acts, in respect of works or other subject-matter, which are not authorised by the rightholder of any copyright or any right related to copyright as provided for by law or the sui generis right provided for in Chapter III of Directive 96/9/EC”. TPM are “deemed ‘effective’ where the use of a protected work or other subject-matter is controlled by the rightholders through application of an access control or protection process, such as encryption, scrambling or other transformation of the work or other subject-matter or a copy control mechanism, which achieves the protection objective.” The content that is access-controlled is not “lawfully accessible” under Art. 4(1) CDSMD.Footnote 111 Point (a) integrates the definition of “effective technological measures” from Art. 6(3) InfoSoc Directive into the Code but focuses on “access controls” with paywalled content and subscription models as examples. Other copyright laws have similar provisions or are interpreted accordingly.Footnote 112 According to Art. 6(4) subpara 1 InfoSoc Directive, “Member States shall take appropriate measures to ensure that rightholders make available to the beneficiary of an exception or limitation provided for in national law the means of benefiting from that exception or limitation to the extent necessary to benefit from that exception or limitation and where that beneficiary has legal access to the protected work or subject-matter concerned”. Per Art. 7(2) CDSMD, this provision also applies to the TDM exception of Art. 4 CDSMD. However, Art. 6(4) does not establish a right to hack. This is also evident from 6(4) Subpara 1 in fine InfoSoc Directive, which includes the condition that the beneficiary must have “legal access to the protected work or subject-matter concerned”. It has to be noted that mere contractual restrictions of web-scraping are not reflected in Measure 1.2., because such restrictions are based per se on contract law, not on EU copyright law.Footnote 113 A measure relating to the exclusion of piracy websites from web-crawling (point b) was already included in previous drafts. However, the final version abandons the term “piracy”Footnote 114 and requires Signatories to fully commit “to exclude from their web-crawling” (1) websites that make available to the public content and (2) which are, at the time of crawling, recognised as persistently and repeatedly infringing copyright and related rights on a commercial scale by courts or public authorities in the European Union and the European Economic Area. Measure 1.2. also states that a dynamic list of hyperlinks to these websites will be made publicly available on an EU website for the purpose of compliance with this measure and to provide greater certainty. First, this measure assumes that content hosted on websites recognised as persistently and repeatedly infringing copyright and related rights on a commercial scale by courts or public authorities in the European Union and the European Economic Area is not “lawfully accessible” for the purpose of Art. 4(1) CDSMD. The argument, posited by some commentators, that lawful access covers any freely available content, irrespective of whether the source is lawful,Footnote 115 is unconvincing because it challenges the very legitimacy of the exception. In other words, there would be no need for an exception if all freely available content could be used for commercial TDM without prior authorisation. We take the view posited by others who argue that “uses from a manifestly unlawful source would not qualify as lawful use.”Footnote 116 Excluding piracy websites from the scope of the TDM exception is a matter of legal fairness and reasonableness, which underlies both copyright law and AI law.Footnote 117 This view is shared in other jurisdictions.Footnote 118 On the other hand, there is no global register of copyright-compliant sources. Signatories are therefore unable to limit automated web-crawling to lawful sources. Such a requirement would amount to a ban on the training of GPAIMs, which would be incompatible with the AI Act’s aim of setting out proportionate rules that foster innovation.Footnote 119 It is for this reason that the full commitment comes with a substantive and a formal condition. The first requires a certain level of infringement that only concerns websites that are “persistently and repeatedly infringing copyright and related rights on a commercial scale”. Isolated and accidental infringements do not suffice. By targeting infringements “on a commercial scale”,Footnote 120 the goal is not to structure the requirement around a subject’s intention, but around a certain threshold of infringement.Footnote 121 These requirements were also applied in the CJEU judgements Stichting BreinFootnote 122 and UPC Telekabel Wien.Footnote 123 The second condition, that the piracy website be “recognised as such by courts or public authorities in the European Union and the European Economic Area”, is a more procedural requirement. It is inspired by EU copyright law providing for injunctions against access providers to block user access to websites persistently and repeatedly infringing copyright and related rights on a commercial scale. Identification or notification of websites by affected rightsholders is therefore insufficient: the piracy status of a website must be recognised by a court or another public authority of a Member State of the EU and the EEA. In most Member States, this is done through a judicial procedure: courts issue site-blocking orders after rightsholders initiate legal proceedings. However, in Greece, Italy and Portugal, the law provides for administrative site-blocking orders. Such administrative procedures are usually faster and less expensive than seeking site-blocking orders from courts.Footnote 124 In light of this diversity of national approaches, Measure 1.2 seeks to make compliance simpler and more secure by referring providers to “a dynamic list of hyperlinks to lists of these websites issued by the relevant bodies in the European Union and the European Economic Area”, which will be made publicly available on an EU website. “Relevant bodies” refers to public authorities and independent bodies such as the “Clearing Body for Copyright on the Internet” in Germany.Footnote 125 Once the list is made available, Signatories must integrate it into their systems and follow it in order to keep it “up to date”, in accordance with Measure 2.1. The respective websites will have to be blacklisted from GPAIM training activities.Footnote 126 2.6 Measure 1.3. Identify and Comply with Rights Reservations When Crawling the World Wide Web (1) In order to help ensure that Signatories will identify and comply with, including through state-of-the-art technologies, machine-readable reservations of rights expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 if they use web-crawlers or have such web-crawlers used on their behalf to scrape or otherwise compile data for the purpose of text and data mining as defined in Article 2(2) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 and the training of their general-purpose AI models, Signatories commit: a) to employ web-crawlers that read and follow instructions expressed in accordance with the Robot Exclusion Protocol (robots.txt), as specified in the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) Request for Comments No. 9309, and any subsequent version of this Protocol for which the IETF demonstrates that it is technically feasible and implementable by AI providers and content providers, including rightsholders, and b) to identify and comply with other appropriate machine-readable protocols to express rights reservations pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790, for example through asset-based or location-based metadata, that have either have been adopted by international or European standardisation organisations, or are state-of-the-art, including technically implementable, and widely adopted by rightsholders, considering different cultural sectors, and generally agreed through an inclusive process based on bona fide discussions to be facilitated at EU level with the involvement of rightsholders, AI providers and other relevant stakeholders as a more immediate solution, while anticipating the development of standards. (2) This commitment does not affect the right of rightsholders to expressly reserve the use of works and other protected subject matter for the purposes of text and data mining pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 in any appropriate manner, such as machine-readable means in the case of content made publicly available online or by other means. Furthermore, this commitment does not affect the application of Union law on copyright and related rights to protected content scraped or crawled from the internet by third parties and used by Signatories for the purpose of text and data mining and the training of their general-purpose AI models, in particular with regard to rights reservations expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790. (3) Signatories are encouraged to support the processes referred to in the first paragraph, points (a) and (b), of this Measure and engage on a voluntary basis in bona fide discussions with rightsholders and other relevant stakeholders, with the aim to develop appropriate machine-readable standards and protocols to express a rights reservation pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790. (4) Signatories commit to take appropriate measures to enable affected rightsholders to obtain information about the web crawlers employed, their robots.txt features and other measures that a Signatory adopts to identify and comply with rights reservations expressed pursuant to Article 4(3) of Directive (EU) 2019/790 at the time of crawling by making public such information and by providing a means for affected rightsholders to be automatically notified when such information is updated (such as by syndicating a web feed) without prejudice to the right of information provided for in Article 8 of Directive 2004/48/EC. (5) Signatories that also provide an online search engine as defined in Article 3, point (j), of Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 or control such a provider are encouraged to take appropriate measures to ensure that their compliance with a rights reservation in the context of text and data mining activities and the training of general-purpose AI models referred to in the first paragraph of this Measure does not directly lead to adverse effects on the indexing of the content, domain(s) and/or URL(s), for which a rights reservation has been expressed, in their search engine. Measure 1.3 has the same scope of application as Measure 1.2 and is subject to the same caveat regarding the applicability of Art. 4 CDSMD.Footnote 127 It also has the same structure including a chapeau and concrete measures. Measure 1.3 is the most comprehensive measure requiring Signatories to identify and comply with rights reservations when crawling the World Wide Web. Its inclusion in the Code was important, considering that this particular issue is expressly mentioned in Art. 53(1)(c) of the AI Act. The Measure seeks to help ensure that Signatories comply with the condition set out in Art. 4(3) CDSMD, which provides that reproductions and extractions of lawfully accessible works and other subject matter for the purposes of text and data mining are permissible on condition that such use “has not been expressly reserved by their rightholders in an appropriate manner, such as machine-readable means in the case of content made publicly available online”. This mechanism is often referred to as an “opt-out,” but from a legal perspective, it is more accurate to refer to it as a limitation of an exception or an exception to an exception.Footnote 128 A valid reservation of rights under Art. 4(3) CDSMD must meet three requirements: (1) the reservation needs to be expressly made, (2) by the right holder, (3) in an appropriate manner. Recital 18 CDSMD suggests that “in the case of content that has been made publicly available online, it should only be considered appropriate to reserve those rights by the use of machine-readable means, including metadata and terms and conditions of a website or a service.” However, “the interpretation of the exact requirement for a valid reservation of rights is an issue for which there are some uncertainties and even competing views.”Footnote 129 While the condition “by the rightsholder” seems rather straight-forward, its application is more complex in situations where multiple parties hold rights in a certain content.Footnote 130 Additionally, the requirement that the reservation be made “in an appropriate manner, such as machine-readable means in the case of content made publicly available online” leaves room for interpretation, including regarding the vocabulary used.Footnote 131 Under copyright law, any “appropriate” reservation of rights must be respected. By contrast, the AI Act introduces a broader, more balanced framework. Article 56(4) of the Act provides that the Code of Practice “take[s] due account of the needs and interests of all interested parties,” including all categories of general-purpose AI providers and rightsholders across cultural and creative sectors. Moreover, per Art. 1(1) AI Act, the Code must maintain a high level of intellectual property protection while also supporting innovation and ensuring proportionality in its obligations. Furthermore, another key challenge lies in scale: GPAIMs are trained on “vast amounts of data” – often comprising billions of tokens. At the same time, many affected rightsholders (such as collective management organisations, publishers, and film or phonogram producers) hold rights in many works and other protected subject matter. No stakeholder in the ecosystem – whether rightsholder or AI provider – can feasibly manage permissions on a granular, right-by-right basis.Footnote 132 To ensure both technical and economic feasibility, standardised mechanisms are necessary to automate rights transactions. Feedback on earlier drafts of the Code demonstrated consensus on this point: rightsholders also ask for standards and “there are strong incentives for both rightsholders and AI model trainers to standardise a relatively small number of identifiers to effectively communicate opt-outs.”Footnote 133 Finally, the purpose of standards is not only to enable operationality but also competitiveness. A fragmented landscape of incompatible or proprietary rights management systems (from providers or rightsholders) risks creating barriers to entry, distorting competition, and undermining the fairness and functionality of the broader AI ecosystem. However, most automatic crawlers do not comply in practice with terms and conditions,Footnote 134 and including non-technical means of rights reservation would engender excessive complexity and ambiguity. Furthermore, some inconsistencies exist between technical and non-technical means of rights reservation in current practices.Footnote 135 Article 3(13) of the Directive (EU) 2019/1024 on open data and the re-use of public sector informationFootnote 136 states that “‘machine-readable format’ means a file format structured so that software applications can easily identify, recognise and extract specific data, including individual statements of fact, and their internal structure”.Footnote 137 “Machine-readable” can be interpreted to include machine-understandable formats,Footnote 138 but the two are not equivalent.Footnote 139 What is needed is immediate machine-to-machine communication at the point and moment of content access.Footnote 140 From the perspective of AI law, and in light of the principle of proportionality, only technical protocols that allow ex ante expression of rights reservations at scaleFootnote 141 should be required.Footnote 142 Measure 1.3 consists of five paragraphs concerning: (1) the Robot Exclusion Protocol (REP, robots.txt) and other appropriate machine-readable protocols; (2) caveats regarding copyright law requirements; (3) the encouragement of Signatories to support the process of developing appropriate machine-readable standards; (4) the obligation of Signatories to provide information to affected rightsholders about their web crawling activities at the time of crawling; and (5) the encouragement of Signatories to ensure that compliance with a rights reservation does not directly lead to adverse effects on indexing in their online search engine (if the Signatory also provides a search engine). The Robot Exclusion Protocol is a broad instruction provided by websites to various “robots” indicating general or specific restrictions and permissions to access and scrape their content. The notion of protocols in this context refers to scalable and technically feasible rights reservation mechanisms, comparable to robots.txt in terms of deployment and effectiveness. This excludes terms and conditions or other textual notices, which, while referenced in Recital 18 of the CDSMD, are not considered protocols in the technical sense. While “it was not originally designed to address copyright management issues”,Footnote 143 “the Robots Exclusion Protocol currently serves as a de facto standard for managing web crawling and scraping activities and has largely been deployed as a primary strategy for TDM rights reservations.”Footnote 144 REP is indeed widely used to block AI crawlers.Footnote 145 Moreover, “current discourse in the industry has pointed towards REP being the benchmark for opt-out provisions.”Footnote 146 Therefore, “website owners can use the REP to instruct web crawlers not to access their site or specific parts of it.”Footnote 147 Some national courts have already accepted robots.txt as a means for rightsholders to express an opt-out in an appropriate manner.Footnote 148 Consequently, “violating the good faith principles of REP by ignoring robots.txt directives or masking their identities by not using known user-agent identifiers or attempting to mimic human traffic (commonly referred as spoofing)”Footnote 149 is ruled out by Measure 1.3(1)(a). However, REP is merely a de facto standardFootnote 150 that ignores natural language instructions.Footnote 151 Under the REP approach, the requirement for rights to be ”expressly“ reserved is interpreted broadly: there is no need to refer to a specific work within a larger collection of content, nor to address a particular user. Rather, rights can be expressed in relation to broader activities such as web scraping.Footnote 152 In order to make the Code future-proof, Measure 1.3(1)(a) extends the REP compliance commitment to “any subsequent version” of the current REP protocol, provided that the Internet Engineering Task Force, which has already started working on setting a standard for AI preferences,Footnote 153 demonstrates it is both technically feasible and practical to implement for AI providers and content providers, including rightsholders. These dual requirements offer Signatories some level of certainty and clarity in implementing an as-yet undefined protocol. While several protocols have been developed or are currently under development – most of them emerging only after November 2022 – their adoption remains uneven.Footnote 154 Importantly, “there are currently no generally recognised standards or protocols for the machine-readable expression of the reservation of rights provided for in Article 4 of the Directive.”Footnote 155 In parallel, the European Commission is considering setting up a unified register for expressing reservations of rights.Footnote 156 It has commissioned a study to explore the feasibility of developing a work-based registry of content identifiers and associated metadata. This registry – whether centralised or based on a federated model – would aim to support the effective expression of rights reservations for copyright-protected works and other subject matter, and to facilitate their identification by AI developers.Footnote 157 Measure 1.3(1)(b) does not refer to any of these solutions specifically but sets out a full commitment “to identify and comply with other appropriate machine-readable protocols to express rights reservations”. This commitment is again subject to substantive and formal conditions. The substantive condition is that, as explained, the rights reservation must be expressed via a scalable machine-readable protocol, for example, through asset-based or location-based metadata.Footnote 158 Asset-based approaches involve metadata that are directly attached to the digital file or dataset. The metadata can express rights reservations, usage preferences, and contact information, and may be permanently embedded through techniques such as digital watermarking.Footnote 159 Work-based solutions, including standards like ISCC and C2PA, also fall within this category. These rely on file-level digital identifiers, metadata, and watermarking, offering rightsholders a much greater degree of granularity in specifying rights reservations or licensing terms. However, such methods are often viewed as more complex to implement. Metadata or watermarks can also be removed or altered, which limits their reliability.Footnote 160 Their effectiveness typically depends on being linked to a registry of rightsholders and their declared preferences.Footnote 161 Location-based approaches, by contrast, function at the level of the server or domain hosting the content. These include top-down mechanisms such as robots.txt, ai.txt, TDMRep, and HTTP response headers.Footnote 162 These solutions are often easier to implement and monitor but offer less precision in rights expression at the level of individual works. In many cases, a combined approach – incorporating both asset- and location-based signals – may be the most effective and realistic solution.Footnote 163 As to the formal condition for compliance with “other” appropriate opt-out protocols, the Measure does not refer to a list of protocols to be published by the Commission.Footnote 164 Instead, it promotes a self-regulatory path towards standardisation, where the Code of Practice serves as both a facilitator and a bridge to future formal standards.Footnote 165 Two alternative paths towards such standards are mentioned. An “appropriate machine-readable protocol” may firstly be “adopted by international or European standardisation organisations” such as the International Organization for Standardization (ISO), the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) or the European Committees for (Electrotechnical) Standardization CEN-CENELEC.Footnote 166 The required formal act of adoption of a protocol as a standard under Measure 1.3(1)(b) must clearly refer to the purpose of the protocol to opt out from TDM for the purpose of GPAI training. The second path towards “other” appropriate opt-out protocols under the Code concerns a “more immediate solution” at the EU level that is meant to “anticipate” the development of regular international or European standards and to promote coherence, trust, and legitimacy, while avoiding fragmentation across Member States.Footnote 167 It presupposes a protocol that is state-of-the-art, technically implementable, and widely adopted by rightsholders, considering different cultural sectors with potentially different needs regarding the expression of an opt-out. Rightsholders, AI providers and other relevant stakeholders must “generally agree” that the protocol at stake fulfils these requirements and thus qualifies as “another” protocol to be identified and complied with per Measure 1.3(1)(b). General agreement does not imply formal consensus but a solution to which most stakeholders can agree, i.e. a situation that is “close to unanimity” across all stakeholder groups.Footnote 168 The inclusive process towards such an outcome may be facilitated at any time “at EU level” by an EU institution. The European Commission may start the EU standardisation process before 2 August 2026 because this is not an enforcement action under the AI Act. In sum, the dual-track approach enshrined in Measure 1.3(1)(b) ensures that the Code remains both forward-looking and pragmatic, allowing for timely implementation without prejudicing the outcomes of longer-term standardisation processes. Measure 1.3.(3) encourages Signatories to actively support all processes outlined in paragraph 1 of this Measure, and to voluntarily engage in bona fide, inclusive discussions with relevant stakeholders – including rightsholders – with the aim of contributing to the development of appropriate machine-readable protocols and standards. Participation in these processes remains voluntary because it does not, in itself, constitute a compliance obligation under copyright or AI law. The first sentence of Measure 1.3(2) clarifies that non-standardised but nonetheless “appropriate” rights reservation mechanisms remain valid under Art. 4(3) CDSMD. Rightsholders retain the freedom to choose among several modes of opt-out,Footnote 169 provided that they are “appropriate” within the meaning of the Directive. Recital 18 CDSMD also further confirms their prerogative to determine how to express such reservations, even in the absence of a formally standardised protocol. Therefore, while the Code only requires standardised protocols, copyright law might require compliance with further modes of opt-out. The second part of Measure 1.3(2) is a reminder that data can be acquired in two main ways: either the Signatory itself conducts web-crawling or obtains pre-existing datasets via third parties – irrespective of whether these datasets are publicly available or sourced through private means.Footnote 170 Third-party dataset providers are not themselves AI model providers and consequently fall outside the scope of the Code.Footnote 171 This fact does not imply, however, that AI providers can ignore the conditions set out in Art. 4 CDSMD by avoiding direct crawling and instead relying on third-party datasets – whether from black or grey markets – that may have been compiled without lawful access, including those sourced from piracy websites, and/or in disregard of rights reservations.Footnote 172 Measure 1.3(2) clarifies that, in these circumstances, Union law on copyright and related rights still applies. The provision concerns any data acquired through means other than the Signatory’s own web-crawling or web-scraping, irrespective of whether the means are commercial, open access, or informal. It is important to note that this provision does not affect authorised uses: datasets obtained through valid licences or agreements with rightsholders remain permissible, as noted in the Recitals, point (d). Measure 1.3(4) complements the Training Data Summary Template,Footnote 173 which is not part of the Code, by establishing a commitment to real time transparency and updates. This measure is particularly important given the practical challenge that website owners face: they would need perfect, real-time knowledge of all crawlers used for machine learning training, and they would need to frequently update their robots.txt files in response to the emergence of new crawlers.Footnote 174 Rightsholders need this information at the moment of crawling,Footnote 175 since that is the critical point at which they must configure or adapt their technical measures, for example, by updating a robots.txt file or implementing a new opt-out protocol.Footnote 176 While some providers do disclose the identities and functionalities of their bots and their features, others do not.Footnote 177 As a result, enforcement is uneven. Under Measure 1.3(4), providers are expected to disseminate real-time updates in two ways: by making public the information specified in Measure 1.3(4) and by providing a means for affected rightsholders to be automatically notified, for instance by syndicating a web feed, when the information is updated. These updates must be immediate. Any significant delay would constitute a failure to properly implement the provider’s copyright policy. These transparency measures are designed to inform and empower affected rightsholders within the meaning of Art. 2(1)(g) of the AI Act. Consequently, holders of EU rights situated in third countries do not benefit from this AI-specific protection.Footnote 178 The final part of the Measure clarifies that it is without prejudice to the right of information provided for in Art. 8 of Directive 2004/48/EC. This again confirms that traditional copyright law principles are unaffected by the Code. Paragraph 5 of Measure 1.3 addresses the ancillary issue of indexing of online content via search engines when the content has been excluded from web-crawling for AI training purposes due to a rights reservation.Footnote 179 It is extremely difficult to establish an objective overview of crawling practices,Footnote 180 and there is a great interest in more nuanced machine-to-machine communication regarding copyright status, reflecting the complex and granular nature of rights management. Existing protocols such as robots.txt were not originally designed with TDM in mind and cannot distinguish between purposes such as AI training, search indexing, or other downstream uses.Footnote 181 In practice, “the crawlers programmed for web scraping are essentially the same as those employed for search indexing: they systematically explore the web by starting with a set of seed URLs and following hyperlinks to discover new pages. This similarity means that a content host may not easily distinguish between a crawler used for search indexing and one used for GenAI data ingestion; moreover, some crawlers serve both functions.”Footnote 182 Multi-purpose crawlers mask the fact that AI actors may collect data for one primary purpose but reuse the collected data for another purpose. Conversely, actors whose robots collect data for a different activity may want to reuse that data for AI without requesting further consent or notifying the owner of the data initially collected.Footnote 183 In particular, news publishers argue that they need to retain visibility in search engines in order to be able to monitor traffic to their websites and their discoverability, while still reserving their rights against use for AI training.Footnote 184 To address these concerns, some AI providers have already deployed separate crawlers for AI data collection and for search-related functions.Footnote 185 Indeed, current practices show that traditional search bots are less frequently excluded: the particularly high omission rates of Internet Archive and Google Search crawlers suggest that web administrators may be open to more traditional crawler uses like in archiving and search engines, even as they seek to restrict AI usage.Footnote 186 Recital 18 of the CDSMD also clarifies that other uses should not be affected by the reservation of rights for the purposes of TDM.Footnote 187 However, from a legal perspective, this issue does not directly concern copyright infringement: if a crawler does not distinguish between purposes and the rightsholder blocks it, neither AI training nor search indexing occurs – therefore, no infringement arises. Conversely, if the rightsholder does not block the crawler, and the content is used for both purposes, the question of whether the absence of blocking constitutes implied consent that legitimises both uses – and thus precludes infringement – remains unresolved in legal doctrine. In either case, the legal implications are uncertain, and the issue appears to fall more within the realm of competition law,Footnote 188 which exceeds the scope of this Code. Therefore, this measure is an encouragement to voluntarily take measures to ensure that a compliance with a rights reservation does not directly lead to adverse effects on the indexing. Currently, the most straightforward way to avoid adverse effects on indexing is having separate crawlers, at least until a more granular opt-out protocol has been standardised, according to paragraph 1(b) of Measure 1.3. 2.7 Measure 1.4. Mitigate the Risk of Copyright-Infringing Output (1) In order to mitigate the risk that a downstream AI system, into which a general-purpose AI model is integrated, generates output that may infringe rights in works or other subject matter protected by Union law on copyright or related rights, Signatories commit: a) to implement appropriate and proportionate technical safeguards to prevent their models from generating outputs that reproduce training content protected by Union law on copyright and related rights in an infringing manner, and b) to prohibit copyright-infringing uses of a model in their acceptable use policy, terms and conditions, or other equivalent documents, or in case of general-purpose AI models released under free and open source licenses to alert users to the prohibition of copyright infringing uses of the model in the documentation accompanying the model without prejudice to the free and open source nature of the license. (2) This Measure applies irrespective of whether a Signatory vertically integrates the model into its own AI system(s) or whether the model is provided to another entity based on contractual relations. While Measures 1.2 and 1.3 aim to ensure compliance with Union copyright law at the development stage of a GPAIM, Measure 1.4 concerns the phase when a GPAIM is used in the EU. Models typically qualify as GPAIMs if their training compute is greater than 1023 FLOP and they can generate text (including code), audio, images or video.Footnote 189 This generative capacity has advanced to a level that equals human creativity. The output of current GPAIMs competes with and has, in some areas such as translations, already replaced human creative works to a significant extent. Beyond this general challenge to the conventional way creative content was created, distributed and consumed,Footnote 190 it has been shown that GPAIMs can generate output that is identical with or recognisably similar to specific, pre-existing works and other subject matter contained in the training dataset.Footnote 191 The prevailing opinion considers such output a reproduction of protected training content, which infringes copyrights or related rights unless an exception or limitation applies.Footnote 192 It is this infringement scenario that Measure 1.4 addresses.Footnote 193 Measure 1.4 has the same structure as Measures 1.2 and 1.3, namely a chapeau that articulates the purpose and scope of application of the measure, and two concrete steps a Signatory must take in order to adhere to the Code and be able to demonstrate compliance with Art. 53(1)(c) AI Act. However, the Measure differs from all other Measures of the Copyright Chapter in that it does not directly regulate potentially infringing activity of a Signatory, but is meant to mitigate a “risk”, namely the risk “that a downstream AI system, into which a general-purpose AI model is integrated” generates infringing output. Art. 3(2) AI Act defines “risk” as the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm.Footnote 194 The relevant harm is the infringing reproduction of training content. The Code is based on the assumption that this infringement does not already occur when a GPAIM is placed on the EU market because an AI model is not in and of itself a reproduction of all protected training content.Footnote 195 Instead, reproductions and possibly communications to the public only occur once a model is used to generate output.Footnote 196 Whether this happens and whether the output is actually infringing (or covered by an exception or limitation) is a future event that is probable, but not entirely certain. Moreover, pursuant to the AI Act, it is not the GPAI “model” that generates the output, but, via a user interface, a downstream “AI system”, into which a GPAIM is integrated.Footnote 197 These AI systems operate, per definition, with “varying levels of autonomy”, and they are often developed and put into service by independent AI system providers.Footnote 198 Last but not least, the output of an AI system depends on the input data (the prompt) submitted by the user who may try to intentionally bring the system to reproduce training content.Footnote 199 For these reasons, Measure 1.4 is limited to two specific risk mitigation measures that a GPAIM provider is able to implement unilaterally at the model layer. Their combined effect should be that no GPAIM is placed on the Union market that can be deployed as an infringement machine that reproduces protected training content at scale. According to point (a), Signatories commit “to implement appropriate and proportionate technical safeguards to prevent their models from generating outputs that reproduce training content protected by Union law on copyright and related rights in an infringing manner”.Footnote 200 The technical safeguards thus have to target “dependent” reproductions, i.e. reproductions of training content,Footnote 201 whereas output that is accidentally identical or substantially similar to a work on which the model was not trained does not call for action.
